title: Headlines from exclusive FT interview with CEO of ASML Christophe Fouquet
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

In an exclusive interview with FT’s Patrick Jenkins, CEO of ASML Christophe Fouquet discusses how he’s built Europe’s biggest business through a total monopoly over the most advanced AI chipmaking equipment.

Key headlines from the interview include:

Fouquet says AI revolution will last 10-15 years: “I think the AI effect on society and industry is going to take 10 to 15 years. We’re only seeing the tip of the iceberg.”

He warns that US pressure to impose an embargo on ASML selling to China could backfire and ultimately create stronger competitors: “We understand that some technology may be restricted for obvious and legitimate concerns, but if we go too far, we are going to create the opposite results of what we’re trying to achieve in the first place,” says Fouquet. Namely, he says, China will be spurred to innovate itself. “If you over-restrict, you bring desperation, and desperation creates a huge appetite for people to accelerate their own technology and, potentially, at some point, become strong competitors.”

The company at the heart of AI has a near-monopoly on the technology needed to make the most advanced chips: ASML has a “total monopoly” on the most advanced EUV lithography machines, which are essential to producing chips for complex AI applications.

Fouquet rejects pressure to maximise profits and says ASML won't exploit its dominant position: “Our profit will grow with the [profits] of the industry, but we are not going to abuse the situation.”

Humanoid robots could be just a few years away: In the interview, Fouquet predicts that “humanoids will be among us . . . a few years from now” and that they will increasingly take on mundane tasks such as gardening and emptying the dishwasher.
Fouquet argues that the success of the world's most strategically important AI infrastructure company comes not from the Silicon Valley model of aggressive competition and winner-takes-all economics, but from long-term investment, extreme collaboration and concentration of expertise.
